items.title: [Kagi Small Web] Books read, August 2026
items.content_html:
Short list for me this month. I did not have a ton of brain for reading, and then the latter part of the month got devoured by 1) preparing for Worldcon and 2) being at Worldcon. (Normally it wouldn't be so bad, but running a table in the dealers' hall entails a lot of stock counting, packing stuff for transport, and prepping ancillary materials like booth decorations.)

Death on the Caldera, Emily Paxman. There's been a minor surge in "fantasy on trains" lately, and I am here for it! Though this one is only briefly on the train, as an accident soon derails it and leaves the characters trying to solve the mystery of both the crash and the ensuing murders while stranded in a hostile environment. I think I wanted a bit more on both the mystery and hostile-environment fronts, but there's not a ton of room to develop those things when you're also dealing with several different magic systems and the politics around witches, who are welcomed and honored in some places and very much not in others, and are almost certainly responsible for the crash.

The witches were an interesting twist! In this world, they're a Jekyll-and-Hyde setup: a normal human woman -- they're all women -- may also have a witch self, which takes over when someone else utters her witch name, and reverts to her human self when that name is spoken instead. It takes time and effort for those two halves to even remember what the other side has been doing, and they're reliant upon/vulnerable to other people switching them back and forth. I feel like it may have been slightly too complicated of a concept to play nice with the plot premise of the crash and subsequent murders, though, at least at the length of this novel; both elements felt a little short-changed by the need to fit in the other material at the same time. This is clearly a setup for a longer series, so possibly, with the groundwork in place, later novels will feel more balanced.

(BTW, I have zero reason to think Paxman read my Doppelganger novels, but the combination of "all witches are women" and "they exist in bifurcated halves" certainly did remind me of those.)

The Library of Amorlin, Kalyn Josephson. Do not go into this expecting much library-ness; the titular Library is much more of a menagerie with some books. That's not a flaw, just something to set your expectations around. ("The Librarian" is admittedly a much more attractive title for the male lead than "the Zookeeper" would be.)

This is an odd world where ordinary animals have nearly gone extinct, replaced by magical beasts that are variously useful and dangerous. Different kingdoms respond to them differently, and the Library is responsible for dealing with problems when beasts wander where they shouldn't be and/or attack humans. The protagonist comes from a realm where beasts are universally hunted and killed; as a criminal, she's been sentenced to the front lines of that fight. But someone approaches her with a deal: if she infiltrates the Library, replacing the woman who's supposed to be sent as the Librarian's new assistant, and helps get the current Librarian removed from power -- thereby furthering the agenda of her kingdom, which hates what the Library stands for -- then she'll be pardoned of her crimes.

Overall I liked the book, but a few things niggled at me. Of course you know going in that Kasira is working for the bad guys and will ultimately not wind up serving their interests, but that pivot takes a while to happen, and I wasn't quite sold well enough on her reasons for staying the course. She's traumatized by being kept in solitary confinement (but not nearly as traumatized as she should be, given that we're told she was there for years) and fears going back, plus she thinks the people at the Library will immediately turn on her when she's unmasked. Which is generally reasonable, but something about the presentation of it just wasn't quite persuasive enough to keep me from being mildly irritated as she passed up one opportunity after another to come clean and ally with the Library.

The narrative also regularly fudges her point of view: more than once, Kasira engineers a situation to ingratiate herself and earn trust from those at the Library, but the reader doesn't know until well into the scene (or even after it) that she arranged the whole thing. I would have liked to see the book use Allaster's viewpoint more often; that would have gotten around that issue while also developing him more as a character -- though then the fact that he's hiding a secret, and the reader doesn't know the full story of it until the end, might have been harder to dodge.

So anyway, I had a lot of quibbles here, but none of them added up to me quitting the book or vowing not to read the sequel. The world is interesting, I want to know what's up with the kingdom that's gone incommunicado, and none of my gripes were deal-breakers.

The Last Contract of Isako, Fonda Lee. I know many people who love the Green Bone Saga, but I am so profoundly allergic to stories about organized crime that I just could not get into Jade City no matter how good the writing was. (Vargo in the Rook and Rose trilogy is Alyc's creation, and the parts of his narrative that focus on the gang end of things were usually not my favorite bits to write.) This book, therefore, gave me a chance to try out something of a different flavor!

Mind you, I'm not super enthused by corporate plots, either, so that bit was an uphill climb. I was more here for the worldbuilding -- especially the fact that Lee commits to and does not back down from the harshness of a more realistic terraforming situation than I normally see in SF. The process takes centuries and is nowhere near being done; in the meanwhile, it's a situation where resources like oxygen and heat are extremely limited. And so people who can no longer contribute to the success of the colony's efforts are incentivized to "resign": they walk out into the lethal landscape, and how far they get before they die is celebrated as a marker for the progress of the terraforming. Their surviving family members get their resignation bonuses, and later, when the domed city expands to encompass where they fell, they're memorialized by having streets and the like named for them.

Of course, this is far from an egalitarian process. The whole planet is a company town, and the directors and board members get to enjoy life-extending treatments or even a second life in a cyborg body, along with greater rations of resources. But even if you were able to transform the colony into a utopia (and this is very much not the kind of story where that's going to happen), there still would fundamentally not be enough resources to go around. And there are other neat elements to the worldbuilding, too, like "kiths" people belong to that form a second kind of non-biological family, and raising kids on behalf of bio-parents is a vital line of work. There's also the weird cognitive dissonance of greenhouse gases being exactly what everybody needs to produce more of, to aid the terraforming efforts.

I've got Breath of the Dragon, Fonda Lee's collaboration with Shannon Lee, on my TBR, and I really need to check that one out -- fantasy being much more my speed than SF!

Humankind: A Hopeful History, Rutger Bregman, trans. Erica Moore and Elizabeth Manton, narr. Rutger Bregman and Thomas Judd. It took me quite a while to get through this one in ebook, but it was worth it.

Bregman's core thesis is that, contrary to all the sources we have telling us that humans are inherently selfish and violent, we're actually inherently generous and kind. The first part of this book systematically works through some of our most famous narratives for People Are Terrible -- Lord of the Flies, the environmental devastation of Rapa Nui, the murder of Kitty Genovese, psych studies like the Stanford Prison Experiment and the Milgram Experiment, etc. -- and debunks them: the actual Tongan boys who wound up in a Lord of the Flies situation survived through intense cooperation and support; Rapa Nui was devastated by rats rather than human wastefulness; people did call in Genovese's murder and were there for her in her final moments; the experiments had a heavy thumb on the scales, misrepresented what the data actually said, or both.

But of course, we do not live in a utopia. So why do people act badly, as they so obviously do? Building on the first part, Bregman shows that many of the usual explanations are wrong. For example, though the Nazis famously claimed they were "just following orders," the actual evidence shows that the leadership were motivated to propose ever-more horrible plans out of a desire to impress Hitler; Milgram's participants were more likely to quit pushing the button when they were nakedly ordered to do so. Most of them kept going because they thought they were making an important contribution to science that would help people in the long run. All too often, bad actions arise out of good impulses: our kindness and generosity, our loyalty to the people around us, can be leveraged to encourage us toward horrible acts.

One of the only bits of received wisdom that still holds water in this book is "power corrupts": yes, it does, absolutely. The minute you put someone in a position of power, the odds that they will begin to abuse it rise noticeably, even if they were a decent person before. And, of course, leadership often attracts people who aren't decent. (The average terrorist is a normal person who thinks they're fighting for a good cause, but the average terrorist leader is a genuine psychopath.)

The final section of the book is simultaneously the most delightful and the hardest to swallow. Bregman turns his attention to efforts that aim to leverage our good qualities, rather than controlling our bad ones: alternative approaches to incarceration and criminal rehabilitation, alternative schools (the usual model is practically designed to produce bullying), alternative corporate structures, etc. These things sound incredibly naive and Pollyanna-ish, and it's hard to wrap your brain around the fact that . . . they work? If you can let go of the feeling that We Need to Punish Criminals, you can massively reduce recidivism and get fewer criminals in the long run. If you stop punching Nazis (which makes them feel tough) and instead turn their annual march into a fundraiser for de-radicalization charities, the Nazis stop marching. A key part of the dismantling of FARC in Colombia literally involved putting Christmas trees out in the forest with notes about how your mother would love for you to come home.

And the narratives matter. I have long been extremely tired of post-apocalyptic worlds that assume an instant and inevitable descent into dog-eat-dog tribalism, because I know that's not what we see during actual disasters. But Bregman also shows how much things like our news media reporting terrible behavior measurably increases terrible behavior, while stories of cooperation and charity up the likelihood that people will cooperate and be charitable. That doesn't mean every story needs to be a cozy thing in which everyone is nice all the time, but it does mean I'm taking a good hard look at what motivations we ascribe to characters and what strategies we show as being successful.

Death on the Cherwell, Mavis Doriel Hay. Sonya Taaffe mentioned this in passing as making a pair with Gaudy Night for mysteries taking place in the same year at fictional Oxford women's colleges, so when I saw the library had it in ebook, I picked it up! This is much slighter than Gaudy Night and not so concerned with having an overt conversation about feminism, scholarship, and so forth, but the first half in particular feels extremely Nancy Drew, in a charming way: a group of undergraduate girls are about to pronounce a hex on their collage's disliked bursar when they find her dead. Ultimately those girls are only part of the investigation, and not the load-bearing one at the end; it is a police officer who finds the culprit, though aided by some information the girls provided. It's a great look at then-contemporary college life, though, from a number of different perspectives.
